strengths: Novel and rigorous theoretical insight: Clear characterization of how ill-conditioned gradients cause grokking delays, with explicit dependence on condition number in Theorem 1
Practical simplicity: Hyperparameter-free, hyperparameter-free drop-in modification with no memory overhead, unlike existing methods like Grokfast
Strong empirical results on algorithmic tasks: Consistent dramatic speedups (grokking in epochs vs. thousands of epochs) across modular arithmetic and sparse parity problems
Clear presentation and motivation: Well-structured paper with effective toy problem analysis (Section 3) that builds intuition before presenting the general method
Principled theoretical grounding: Establishes connection to natural gradient descent (Equation 13), showing EGD as a whitened NGD variant
weaknesses: Severe theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 applies only to specific toy setting (linear model, 2D folded Gaussian); zero formal guarantees for the proposed EGD method on neural networks
Extremely limited experimental scope: Only algorithmic tasks tested; no experiments on naturalistic grokking (vision, language) despite these being mentioned in introduction as important
Column normalization performs similarly to EGD in experiments (Figures 1-3), yet paper doesn't adequately explain why full EGD is necessary over simpler alternatives—critical ablation missing
Scalability not addressed: SVD is O(m²p) per step; no wall-clock timing analysis, computational overhead quantification, or study of randomized approximations despite acknowledging them
Incomplete comparisons with related work: Section 4.2 argues advantages over Grokfast but provides no direct experimental comparison; no comparison with other optimizers (Adam, LayerNorm, etc.)
Missing methodological guidance: Unclear which layers practitioners should apply EGD to; no principled layer-selection strategy provided; rank deficiency handling not discussed
Insufficient ablations and analysis: No investigation of when EGD helps vs. doesn't; no sensitivity to SVD approximation quality; Figure 6 robustness only on toy problem

strengths: Clear pedagogical motivation through analytically solvable toy problem (Theorem 1, Corollary 1) that elegantly demonstrates how ill-conditioned gradients cause grokking plateaus
Remarkably simple, practical method (single SVD transformation) with no hyperparameters, no additional memory, and no scheduling requirements
Strong, consistent empirical results on standard grokking benchmarks (sparse parity, modular arithmetic) where method eliminates/drastically reduces plateau duration
Well-articulated connections to natural gradient descent and clear comparison with Grokfast, delineating advantages in memory efficiency, simplicity, and theoretical guarantees
Excellent presentation with clear structure, intuitive figures (especially Figure 4 on ill-conditioned spectra), and honest acknowledgment of limitations
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental scope restricted to small synthetic problems only (n≤400 for parity, p≤127 for modular arithmetic, networks with ≤512 hidden units); no experiments on naturalistic tasks despite citations to grokking on vision/language datasets

Substantial theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 applies only to linear model with engineered data distribution; connection to neural networks is purely empirical, leaving unexplained why identical mechanism works across diverse architectures/tasks
Missing critical direct experimental comparison with Grokfast, the most relevant baseline claiming grokking acceleration; Grokfast only appears in initial figures with unclear experimental setup

Computational cost analysis absent: full SVD per layer per iteration is O(min(mp², m²p)); no wall-clock measurements, no validation of 'SVD doesn't need to be precise' claim, scalability to large models undemonstrated
Grokking detection mechanism for switching from EGD to vanilla SGD is unexplained, introducing undocumented hyperparameter that somewhat undermines 'hyperparameter-free' claim
Limited ablation studies: no analysis of column normalization variant's effectiveness, approximate SVD degradation, layer-specific application, or rank-deficiency handling mentioned in Remark 1
No statistical significance testing with error bars or multiple random seeds; single-run results without variance estimates
Unaddressed disconnect between toy problem using quadratic loss and experiments using cross-entropy/hinge loss; finite-sample behavior not analyzed despite w.h.p. theoretical statements

strengths: Clear motivation and intuitive explanation: The toy problem in Section 3 elegantly demonstrates why ill-conditioned gradients cause O(1/ε) plateaus, with excellent visualization (Figure 4) of gradient spectra evolution
Principled theoretical analysis: Theorem 1 rigorously characterizes grokking dynamics in the simplified setting, with explicit phase diagrams quantifying plateau lengths
Simple and practical method: Hyperparameter-free spectral normalization that elegantly unifies natural gradient descent interpretation; clear algorithmic description enables reproducibility

Comprehensive experimental validation: Multi-scale experiments spanning toy problems, algorithmic tasks (modular arithmetic, sparse parity), realistic datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10), multiple architectures (MLPs, CNNs, transformers), and multiple optimizers
Dramatic empirical speedups on core domain: 45x acceleration on modular arithmetic with immediate grokking is compelling evidence; clear improvements on primary benchmark tasks

Honest scientific reporting: Transparently discusses limitations including SVD instability on transformers (Figures 14-15), RSVD rank tuning requirements, and convergence to different parameter regions (Appendix F)
Well-positioned connections: Clearly relates to natural gradient descent, provides connections to Grokfast and Muon, and engages with recent mechanistic interpretation literature
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: Core contribution applies known spectral preconditioning technique (related to natural gradient descent via Eq. 13) to a new domain rather than introducing novel optimization machinery; for a top venue, more technical innovation expected

Severe theory-practice gap: Theoretical analysis (Section 3, Appendix A) restricted to linear models with quadratic loss and specific Gaussian data distributions; completely absent for nonlinear networks where grokking is actually studied; claims of 'effective theory' overstated

Incomplete mechanistic understanding: While correlating ill-conditioning with delayed generalization, paper doesn't explain the sharp memorization→generalization phase transition central to grokking phenomenon; doesn't clarify when/how generalizing circuits emerge

Mixed and inconclusive practical results: On realistic settings, performance is inconsistent with claims—MNIST (Table 6): Grokfast 28.7s vs EGD 11.7s (requires rank tuning); Transformer+Modulo (Table 7): Grokfast 114.0s vs EGD(RSVD) 129.3s; often Grokfast comparable or superior, contradicting positioning

Hyperparameter-free claim undermined: Exact SVD unstable on transformers necessitating RSVD; rank selection requires task-specific tuning (ranges from r=4 to r=64 across experiments) with no principled selection guidance, directly contradicting 'hyperparameter-free' positioning

Converges to different solutions: Appendix F shows EGD and vanilla SGD reach different parameter regions (particularly on modular arithmetic), raising concerns about robustness/transferability differences and suggesting the acceleration mechanism differs from stated conditioning normalization hypothesis

Unfair Grokfast comparison: Claims theoretical guarantees vs. Grokfast's heuristic nature, but theoretical guarantees don't transfer to practical nonlinear settings; memory advantage claimed but not quantified; wall-clock time often disadvantages EGD due to higher per-step SVD cost; omits recent Grokfast variants

strengths: Clear intuition through well-designed toy problem (Section 3) that motivates the method via ill-conditioned gradient spectra
Rigorous theoretical analysis (Theorem 1, Corollary 1) showing plateau length scales as O(1/ε) for the toy problem
Simple, practical algorithm with no hyperparameters, no extra memory, and easy integration into training loops
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across diverse settings (modular arithmetic, sparse parity, MNIST, CIFAR-10, multiple architectures and optimizers)
Thoughtful ablations and variants (exact SVD, randomized SVD, column normalization) with computational efficiency analysis
Strong exposition of connections to natural gradient descent (Eq. 13) and independent convergence with Muon optimizer
Excellent reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, pseudo-code, and promised code release
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the core transformation is essentially Fisher preconditioning (a standard technique); the innovation is primarily in application rather than methodology
Significant theory-practice gap: Theorem 1 applies only to 2D linear toy problem; convergence analysis for practical non-linear networks remains unresolved ('highly difficult')
Unclear mechanism generalization: insufficient evidence that ill-conditioning is the primary cause of grokking across all tested problems; only Figure 4 demonstrates one example

Stability concerns: Figures 14-15 show EGD with exact SVD becomes highly unstable for transformers on modular multiplication; RSVD fixes this but requires rank tuning, undermining 'hyperparameter-free' claims
Missing failure case analysis: column normalization and some RSVD variants fail on sparse parity k=4 with no principled explanation or diagnostic guidance

Mixed practical results vs Grokfast: MNIST (Table 6) shows marginal improvements (~0.9% better accuracy); transformers (Table 7) show Grokfast is faster with exact SVD; competitive performance requires RSVD rank tuning
Computational overhead not justified: wall-clock time results (Tables 2-4) show simpler column normalization often wins despite being 'simplified' EGD, and SVD adds non-trivial cost per iteration
Incomplete solution analysis: EGD converges to different parameter regions than vanilla SGD (Appendix F) with limited discussion of implications for generalization or solution preferences
Rank selection for RSVD: task-dependent optimal rank with no principled a priori selection method, introducing hyperparameter sensitivity contrary to claimed simplicity
Limited scope: strongest results on synthetic algorithmic problems; real-world grokking (vision, NLP mentioned in intro) lacks experimental support; MNIST/CIFAR-10 results show mixed performance
Practical guidance gap: no clear decision framework for practitioners on when to use EGD vs Grokfast, or which variant (SVD/RSVD/column norm) to choose

Presentation: extended length with key results in appendices; non-stationarity experiments (Appendix E) feel disconnected; toy problem (infinite samples, exact statistics) vs practical finite-sample networks gap could be clearer
